docs.title: make_server(port=8765)
docs.text:
Bind to 127.0.0.1 only, trying the next ports if the first is busy.

Source code in src/bridge_island/ui.py 
def make_server(port: int = 8765) -> tuple[ThreadingHTTPServer, App]:
    """Bind to 127.0.0.1 only, trying the next ports if the first is busy."""
    last: OSError | None = None
    for candidate in range(port, port + 20) if port else [0]:
        app = App(candidate)
        try:
            server = _Server(("127.0.0.1", candidate), make_handler(app))
        except OSError as exc:
            last = exc
            continue
        app.port = server.server_address[1]
        return server, app
    raise OSError(f"no free port from {port} to {port + 19}: {last}")

docs.title: Using the app (no command line)
docs.text: bridge-island has a point-and-click app that opens in your web browser. You choose what should happen in a simulated run, press a button, and get the result explained in plain sentences, with tables, charts and downloads. All content is invented and all numbers are synthetic, illustrative.

docs.title: Start it
docs.text:
Windows: double-click Start-bridge-island.bat in the project folder. A black window opens and your browser opens the app. Leave the black window open while you use the app.

To get a shortcut on your desktop, right-click Start-bridge-island.bat, choose Send to, then Desktop (create shortcut).

Any system: the same thing from a terminal is uv run bridge-island ui (or python -m bridge_island ui). Add --no-browser if you do not want the browser to open, and --port N to choose the first port to try.

The first time you start it, uv may take a minute to set up the project. After that it starts in a second or two. You need uv installed once.

Stop it by closing the black window (or pressing Ctrl+C in it).

docs.title: What you will see
docs.text:
The page across the top has six tabs.

Tab What it is for Run a simulation Choose an example, how long to run, how the Bridge behaves, and what goes wrong (a stall, a faulty system). The Quick starts fill the form with common cases. Scenario files Run one of the shipped scenarios, or paste your own. A scenario file describes one run completely, so it can be shared and repeated. Full report One page with everything for an example. Open it here, or download it as a single file that works offline. Check the guidelines Runs a test for each of the six design guidelines and says pass or fail, in words. Experiments The four repeatable experiments, with tables, plots and downloadable files. Help Plain-English explanations of every term, how to read the charts, and the scenario file format.

docs.title: Reading a result
docs.text:
• The tiles across the top are the headline: how many systems are OK, how much was delivered, the worst peak age, how many deliveries were late, how many messages were blocked, and how many things the Bridge noticed. A coloured edge plus a word shows whether to look closer.
  • What happened says the same in sentences.
  • How each system fared has one row per system with a status (a tick for OK, a triangle for Watch, a cross for Problem; never colour alone), the reason, and two bars on one shared scale: Average age is how old the system's newest value was on average over the whole run, and Peak age is the oldest it ever got. A system can look fine at arrival and still hold old data, so read both (how age is measured).
  • Age of the data over time has one chart per system. Across is when the data arrived; up is how old it was. Hollow markers are estimates, and systems use different marker shapes.
  • What the Bridge noticed counts the events by kind, then lists them. Show the full table opens every number behind the board.
  • Keep the results downloads what you need: the numbers (JSON), every datum (CSV), the settings as a scenario file you can run again, and a record of how to reproduce the run.
  • The form is repeated under the result, filled in with what you chose, so you can change one thing and run again. The same seed always gives the same result.

docs.title: Things to try
docs.text:
1. Press Run with the defaults. Read What happened.
  2. Press the quick start The Bridge stalls for 1.5 s. Find the sentence about the health monitor, and the dot high on the chart for the system that holds data longest.
  3. Try Stamp data with delivery time (the error). The stall is still there, but nothing is flagged late, because old data now looks new. This is why the design keeps the original time (guideline G3).
  4. Try Baseline v2 removes an element. One system is told that an input is no longer available, instead of quietly going without it.
  5. Try A faulty system sends bad messages. The Bridge blocks the message and the baseline never sees it.
  6. Open Check the guidelines and run it on both examples.

docs.title: Is it safe?
docs.text: The app runs only on your own computer. It listens on the loopback address 127.0.0.1, so other machines cannot reach it, and it sends nothing anywhere. Every form carries a one-time token for the session, the address the browser used is checked, and nothing you type is ever used as a file name: scenarios are chosen from the shipped list or pasted as text, and results are kept in memory and only written to disk when you press a download button. Do not expose it to a network.

docs.title: If it does not start
docs.text:
What you see What to do "bridge-island could not start" in the black window Install uv and double-click the file again. The browser did not open Copy the address printed in the black window (it looks like http://127.0.0.1:8765/) into your browser. The address in the window is not 8765 Another program had that port, so the app used the next free one. Use the address it prints. "This page has expired" The app was restarted. Reload the page and try again. Your security software blocks it The app only talks to your own computer. Allow Python or uv to run, or run uv run bridge-island ui from a terminal.

The app is for learning, demonstration and research. It is not flight or medical software and is not certified. See Design rationale and limitations.

docs.title: Command-line reference
docs.text:
Every command works from a checkout of the repository (the examples live in examples/). All content is invented and all numbers are synthetic, illustrative. Run bridge-island --help or bridge-island <command> --help for the options.

Command What it does list Lists the examples, their baseline versions and subsystems, and the shipped scenarios. demo EXAMPLE Runs an example on both baseline versions, then compares what the change costs with point to point. describe EXAMPLE Shows the baseline interface, the unique systems and every mapped path, as text, Markdown, Mermaid or JSON. diff EXAMPLE Shows what a baseline version change touches, measured on the real mapping files. run SCENARIO.yaml Runs one reproducible scenario described in YAML. See Scenarios. report EXAMPLE Writes one self-contained HTML report. check-rules Runs the checks for guidelines G1 to G6 and prints pass or fail. experiment NAME Runs one of the four experiments, writing CSV and plots. codegen --spec FILE Compiles a YAML mapping spec to a Python module (G5).

docs.title: A short tour
docs.text:
uv run bridge-island list
uv run bridge-island demo aviation
uv run bridge-island describe aviation --version 2
uv run bridge-island diff aviation
uv run bridge-island run examples/scenarios/stall_and_resume.yaml
uv run bridge-island report aviation --out report.html --stall 2.2,1.5

docs.title: describe
docs.text:
$ bridge-island describe aviation --version 2
aviation: baseline interface v2 (all content invented; numbers are synthetic, illustrative)
13 published elements, 4 unique subsystems, 18 paths: 10 identity, 7 converted, 1 removed
...
  NavigationState.altitude         ->  PlanningDisplay.nav_alt_m         identity
  NavigationState.altitude         ->  StatusLogger.altitude_ft          unit m->ft
  AirData.baro_altitude_ft         ->  CueingProcessor.baro_alt_m        REMOVED: element removed ...

--format mermaid prints a flowchart you can paste into any Mermaid renderer, including the diagram support in this documentation. --format json gives the same data for scripts.

docs.title: diff
docs.text: bridge-island diff aviation lists the interface changes between two baseline versions and then shows the change on the Bridge as it actually is: the number of substantive lines that change in the mapping spec (comments and blank lines are not counted), and the unified diff. For the aviation example the measured change is +11 / -8 lines in one file, and the only unique system affected is the one that used the removed element. The modelled P2P-versus-Bridge counts follow, with the caveats in Experiments. --from and --to choose the versions; --full prints the whole diff.

docs.title: report
docs.text:
Writes one HTML file that you can open offline, e-mail or print. It contains the architecture, the G1 to G6 results for every baseline version, a table of what each unique system received (age at arrival, average age over time, peak age), a chart per system of the age of its data, the full mapping with identity and converted paths marked, the Bridge's event log, and what the version change touches. Options: --seed, --duration, --rate-policy cap|extrapolate, and --stall AT,DURATION to stall the Bridge during the run.

The file has no scripts and loads nothing from the network. Charts are inline SVG with a title and a text description, and they use marker shapes as well as colour (hollow markers are estimates). The page follows the reader's light or dark setting, and the report is deterministic: the same options, with the same package and Python versions, give the same file.

docs.title: Machine-readable output
docs.text:
list, demo, describe, diff, run and check-rules accept --json (or --format json). JSON goes to stdout and nothing else does: messages such as wrote summary.json go to stderr, so the output can be piped straight into other tools.

uv run bridge-island run examples/scenarios/fault_injection.yaml --json | python -m json.tool

docs.title: Colour
docs.text: PASS and FAIL are coloured only when the output is a terminal. Colour is switched off by --no-color, by the NO_COLOR environment variable, by TERM=dumb, and when output is piped or redirected. FORCE_COLOR=1 switches it on.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 Success. 1 A check failed: a guideline rule did not pass, or the code generator rejected a spec. 2 Invalid input or usage: a bad scenario file, an unknown version, a bad option. The message says what to fix.

docs.title: Rate policy
docs.text: demo, report and scenario files accept a rate policy for subsystems that can use a higher rate than the baseline sends: cap (the default) or extrapolate. Neither policy gives the subsystem what it asked for; see Concepts.

docs.title: The two islands
docs.text:
Term Meaning Baseline Island The host platform. It is immutable to the integrator and certified by another authority. Only its published interface may be used. Unique Island The integrator's own mission systems. Each has its own native interface, protocol, units and rates, and evolves independently. Bridge The single mediation layer. It is the only path between the islands. Point-to-point (P2P) The comparison architecture: each unique system is wired directly to the baseline elements it needs.

The baseline is certified and owned elsewhere, so the integrator cannot change it. The unique systems are owned and changed by different teams on different schedules. Without a mediator, every unique system carries its own copy of the knowledge of how to talk to the baseline. That knowledge is spread over as many places as there are systems, and each copy must be updated when the baseline changes.

docs.title: The Bridge, and what is in it
docs.text:
The Bridge is one object (bridge_island.bridge.Bridge) with five parts.

Part Role OEM Interface Unit (OIU) Faces the baseline. It follows the baseline's published interface exactly, and acts as a remote terminal toward the baseline. Translator Module (TM) Holds all format, content and protocol conversion, and the time-tag handling. Unique Interface Distributor (UID) Keeps a separate connection to each unique system, in that system's own native format. It acts as the controlling side toward the unique systems. Health monitor A background service. It detects stale data and stall-and-resume discontinuities, and annunciates them to the affected systems. Cyber monitor A background service. It enforces which data may cross, and in which direction. 
sequenceDiagram
    participant BL as Baseline (bus controller)
    participant OIU
    participant TM as Translator Module
    participant UID
    participant U as Unique system
    BL->>OIU: message, valid at time t (commanded transfer)
    OIU->>TM: message (published elements only)
    TM->>UID: datum in the system's units, still tagged t
    UID->>U: native protocol (bus, label words or pub/sub)
    Note over U: age = now - t
    U->>UID: request (native format)
    UID->>TM: cyber monitor allows? then translate
    TM->>OIU: baseline message
    BL->>OIU: poll for pending input
    OIU-->>BL: the message

docs.title: Role asymmetry
docs.text:
The baseline's bus has a bus controller (BC) that starts every transfer, and remote terminals (RTs) that only answer. The OIU is an RT. It cannot push data to the baseline; it can only hold a message until the baseline polls for it. The baseline stays in control of its own bus, and the Bridge fits into the role the baseline already defines.

Toward the unique side the roles flip. The UID is the controlling side: bus controller on a command/response bus, sole transmitter on a label-word bus, publisher on a pub/sub bus. The Bridge therefore decides when each unique system hears from it, and a unique system cannot start a conversation with the baseline.

docs.title: The six design guidelines
docs.text:
Each guideline is implemented as runtime behavior and checked by tests whose names start with the guideline number (for example test_g3_source_time_preserved). bridge-island check-rules runs the same checks on an example and prints pass or fail.

G1. Complete retargeting. No unique system has a direct link to the baseline. The baseline platform refuses to attach anything that does not declare itself part of a Bridge, and a network registry records every link so that a bypass can be found by inspection. Python cannot make a bypass literally impossible for code that lies about what it is, so the guarantee is "impossible through the public API, and detected otherwise". The P2P module turns the refusal off on purpose, and the registry then reports one bypass link per subsystem.

G2. Translate only where needed. When the baseline and unique representations of an element have the same encoding, units and frame, the datum passes through unchanged under an identity transform. The code generator rejects a mapping that lists a conversion where none is needed, and rejects one whose conversions do not reach the target representation.

G3. Time-tag integrity. Each datum carries the source time of validity, never the Bridge's delivery time. The Bridge adds latency, and a consumer can always compute data age as now - source_time. The Translator Module has a deliberately naive delivery mode that stamps arrival time instead, to show the error: a datum held inside the Bridge for a second arrives looking brand new.

G4. Baseline immutability. The OIU accepts only messages and elements the baseline publishes, and emits only messages the baseline is specified to accept. Anything else is rejected and logged inside the Bridge. The Bridge refuses to start if its mapping refers to an element the baseline does not publish.

G5. Compiled mapping. The baseline-to-unique mapping is a YAML spec. bridge-island codegen turns it into a Python module at build time, with straight-line conversion code and no run-time tables. Every generated file begins with a header naming the spec and its SHA-256:

# GENERATED FILE - DO NOT EDIT.
# Generated by bridge-island codegen from spec: mapping_v2.yaml
# Spec SHA-256: <hex digest of the spec>

The only conversions a spec can name are the permitted transforms: identity, scale and offset, unit conversion, enum mapping, bit-field pack and unpack, binary-angle encode and decode, and range checks.

G6. Single-unit realization. One Bridge object composes the OIU, TM, UID and monitors. Mixed criticality is handled by separation inside the object: each part sits in a named partition (baseline-facing, translation, unique-facing, monitor), and the parts hold no direct references to each other. They communicate only through callbacks owned by the Bridge.

docs.title: How age is measured
docs.text:
G3 keeps the source time, so a receiver can always compute age. There are three useful ways to summarize it, and they answer different questions. In the vocabulary of temporal databases, source time is valid time (when the fact was true in the world) and delivery time is closer to transaction time (when the system learned it). Age of information as a measure of freshness is from the networking literature (see Related work).

Measure Question it answers Age at arrival How old was a datum at the moment it landed? Average age over time If a receiver looks at its data at a random moment, how old is it on average? Peak age How old does the data it holds get, at worst, just before the next update? Time out of tolerance For how long was the data older than the receiver says it can accept?

Age at arrival ignores the time a receiver spends holding a datum while it waits for the next one. For a stream delivered every T seconds with delay d, the average age over time is d + T/2 and the peak is d + T. An update only resets the age if it is fresher than what is already held, so an old datum arriving late does not make the data look younger. Estimates are aged from the real sample they are based on.

For the invented aviation example, 8 simulated seconds, seed 1 (synthetic, illustrative):

Subsystem Age at arrival Average over time Peak Same run with a 1.5 s Bridge stall: peak PlanningDisplay (5 Hz) 8.5 ms 108.5 ms 208.5 ms 1708.0 ms CueingProcessor (up to 50 Hz) 6.7 ms 28.8 ms 106.7 ms 1606.2 ms VoiceRelay (1 Hz) 6.7 ms 506.6 ms 1006.7 ms 1706.2 ms StatusLogger (1 Hz) 1005.5 ms 1505.5 ms 2005.5 ms 2005.5 ms

VoiceRelay is the instructive row. Its data arrives 6.7 ms old, which looks excellent, but because it gets an update only once a second its data is on average 507 ms old over time. And during a stall, PlanningDisplay still reports an age at arrival near 10 ms while the data it holds gets 1.7 s old. Arrival-only figures miss that, so the app and the report show all of these measures. A subsystem's own tolerance (stale_after_s) is used for the last one: in the stalled run, CueingProcessor, which tolerates 0.25 s, spent 1.36 s working from data older than it accepts.

docs.title: Data age, rates and what the Bridge does not do
docs.text:
• A subsystem declares the highest rate it can use. When the baseline sends faster than that, the Bridge drops samples to stay at the subsystem's rate. When the baseline sends slower, the Bridge follows one of two rate policies, chosen when the Bridge is built (rate_policy="cap" or "extrapolate"; on the command line, bridge-island demo aviation --rate-policy extrapolate).

    cap (default) extrapolate What the subsystem receives Only real samples, at the baseline's rate One item per period of its own rate: the freshest real sample, or else an estimate Estimates None Linear for floats, held for integer codes, enums and booleans; never beyond a time limit after the last real sample (default: 1.5 periods of that input's source, or set max_extrapolation_s), so a dead source is not masked Marking n/a Every estimate has estimated=True and a basis_time; its age is measured from the real sample it is based on Example below 20 per second 49.8 per second, 60% estimated Age of real samples 6.7 ms 21.7 ms (they wait for their slot) Oldest delivery 6.7 ms 56.7 ms (an estimate is as old as its basis) Largest estimate error n/a 0.8 mm Subsystem's 50 ms latency budget Met Missed: the subsystem flags the old estimates

    The example is the invented aviation CueingProcessor, which wants altitude at 50 Hz with a 50 ms latency budget, fed from a 20 Hz baseline source (synthetic, illustrative, 10 s run). Neither policy gives the subsystem what it asked for. The baseline does not send 50 Hz data, and no policy can create it. cap supplies real data at the rate that exists, within the latency budget. extrapolate supplies the rate the interface expects, at the cost of predicted values and added latency. Both keep the existing interface working. The subsystem's owner has to decide which compromise it can live with. * A baseline element that is removed is not guessed at. The generated mapping records it, the Bridge logs it, and the UID tells the affected subsystem that the input is unavailable. See the aviation example. * The buses are simplified behavioral models inspired by public avionics bus concepts (command/response, label words, publish/subscribe). They are not implementations of any standard.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Thanks for your interest. Bug reports, questions, new invented examples and documentation fixes are welcome.

docs.title: Ground rules
docs.text:
1. Invented content only. Every platform, message, field, rate and number must be invented and generic. Do not add real aircraft, program, supplier, company or product names, real interface control documents, bus addresses, data rates or program metrics. scripts/release_check.py enforces this and runs in CI.
  2. Label any numeric output "synthetic, illustrative".
  3. Use Conventional Commits (feat:, fix:, docs:, test:, chore:).
  4. Disclose AI assistance in docs/AI_USAGE.md if you used it.

docs.title: Development setup
docs.text:
uv sync --all-groups
uv run pre-commit install
uv run pytest
uv run ruff check . ; uv run ruff format --check .
uv run mypy
uv run python scripts/release_check.py

Two heavier checks are not part of the normal run:

uv run python scripts/mutation_check.py --sample 300 --jobs 4   # does a test notice each deliberate break?
uv run --with bandit bandit -q -r src -ll                        # security scan (one known false positive is marked)

mutation_check.py changes the code on purpose (< to <=, + to -, a constant by one ...) and reports every change that no test noticed. If you add behaviour, add a test that fails when it is broken. Please also read docs/rationale.md ("Critical review"), which lists what the evidence here does and does not show.

Everything is cross-platform. Helper tasks are Python scripts, not shell scripts.

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text: Keep them small and focused. Add or update tests. Tests for the design guidelines are named after them (for example test_g3_source_time_preserved).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Both examples live in examples/. Each has a world.py (the platforms and subsystems), mapping_v1.yaml and mapping_v2.yaml (the mapping specs), and generated/ (the compiled mappings). Every name, field, rate and number is invented.

uv run bridge-island demo aviation
uv run bridge-island demo medical
uv run bridge-island check-rules --example medical

docs.title: Aviation: Generic Host Air Vehicle (GHAV)
docs.text:
The baseline (command/response bus) publishes:

Message Elements Rate (v1) NavigationState latitude, longitude, altitude, heading, groundspeed 20 Hz AirData barometric altitude, airspeed 10 Hz AttitudeState roll, pitch, yaw 50 Hz PowerStatus bus voltage, power state 1 Hz TimeReference UTC seconds 1 Hz

and accepts one input, DisplayRequest. The Unique Island has four subsystems with deliberately different native interfaces:

Subsystem Native interface What it shows PlanningDisplay publish/subscribe, high latency tolerance Metric units, 5 Hz. Sends show_page requests upward. CueingProcessor label words Position and attitude in radians, tight latency budget. VoiceRelay label words The tightest latency budget. StatusLogger command/response Already speaks the baseline representation, so every path is an identity (G2).

docs.title: Baseline v1 to v2
docs.text:
Baseline v2 applies one change of each kind:

Kind Change rename NavigationState.groundspeed_kt becomes ground_speed_kt unit NavigationState.altitude changes from feet to meters encoding NavigationState.heading changes from a 16-bit binary angle to float degrees rate AttitudeState goes from 50 Hz to 100 Hz added NavigationState.vertical_speed_mps (nothing uses it) removed AirData.baro_altitude_ft

What happens, with the files you would edit:

  • Everything but the removal is absorbed by mapping_v2.yaml. No unique system is edited. PlanningDisplay's altitude and heading used to need conversions and now pass through unchanged; StatusLogger used to pass altitude through and now needs a meters-to-feet conversion. The faster attitude rate is absorbed by the UID, which keeps delivering at each subsystem's own cap.
  • The removal is visible, not silent. CueingProcessor used the barometric altitude. The mapping marks that entry status: removed. The Bridge logs it at start-up, and the UID tells CueingProcessor that baro_alt_m is unavailable. CueingProcessor.check() then reports baro_alt_m: unavailable (element removed from baseline interface v2). If the entry were left as it was, the code generator would fail the build instead.
  • A Bridge built for v1 refuses to run against v2. It raises InterfaceMismatch and lists what no longer fits.
  • The same change on point-to-point shows the failure the Bridge avoids: with each subsystem's adapter still written for v1, PlanningDisplay converts the altitude from feet to meters when it is already in meters, and no error is raised. The renamed field is a lookup failure inside each adapter. Nothing tells CueingProcessor that the barometric altitude is gone. It simply stops receiving it. (tests/test_p2p.py::test_p2p_adapters_written_for_v1_break_silently_on_v2.)

docs.title: Medical device: Generic Infusion Host Platform (GIHP)
docs.text:
The same pattern applies wherever a certified core must interoperate with independently evolving peripherals under separate authority. Here a cleared host platform (the Baseline Island) publishes pump state, alarm state and a device clock, and accepts one display request. Three add-on modules make up the Unique Island:

Subsystem Native interface What it needs DoseAdvisor publish/subscribe Flow in litres per hour, pressure in psi. BedsideDisplay publish/subscribe The baseline's own units, a named pump mode. Sends show_view requests upward. AlarmRelay label words Alarm code, priority and active flag, with a tight latency budget.

Baseline v2 renames volume_infused_ml to total_volume_ml, changes line pressure from kPa to mmHg, turns the numeric alarm code into a named value, doubles the alarm-state rate, adds a battery-level element, and removes the alarm priority. The result has the same shape as the aviation example: the mapping absorbs the changes, and the removal is reported to AlarmRelay.

Note

This example is a structural illustration. It makes no clinical claim, models no real device, and is not medical software. No real product or company is represented.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
Four experiments demonstrate the structural argument. They are seeded and write CSV files, and plots too when matplotlib is installed (uv sync --extra plots).

Synthetic, illustrative

Every number on this page and in the output files is synthetic and illustrative. The experiments run on invented platforms with stated counting models. They show how the two architectures behave in a structural argument. They are not program data and they do not predict any real program's outcome. Each CSV starts with the line # synthetic, illustrative.

Each experiment has a CLI command and a script that does the same thing:

uv run bridge-island experiment <topology|change-impact|timing|containment> [--seed N] [--out DIR] [--example aviation|medical]
python experiments/topology_sweep.py      # also: change_impact.py, timing_continuity.py, fault_containment.py

Output goes to DIR/<experiment>/ (default outputs/). The same seed gives byte-identical files.

docs.title: 1. Topology sweep
docs.text:
uv run bridge-island experiment topology --seed 1

Sweeps the number of baseline elements n and unique subsystems m, with a configurable dependency density (the chance that a given subsystem uses a given element), and counts interfaces:

Architecture Interfaces P2P E, the number of dependency edges; worst case n * m Bridge n + m Bridge, baseline side consolidated onto one interface 1 + m

Files: topology_sweep.csv, topology_sweep.png. For n = 40 and density 0.3 the run gives (P2P column is the mean of 5 repeats):

m P2P (E) P2P worst case Bridge n + m Bridge 1 + m 2 25.2 80 42 3 4 47.4 160 44 5 8 93.2 320 48 9 16 187.8 640 56 17

What n counts

In this repository n is the number of baseline data elements (fields of published messages), and |E| counts element-level dependencies: one per (element, subsystem) pair. It is not the number of baseline systems or units. A count at the level of systems would be much smaller than these, so the numbers here are not comparable with counts taken at another level.

At this density and size the Bridge does not win at every point. With 2 subsystems, point-to-point needs fewer interfaces than the Bridge's + m (25.2 against 42); with 4 they are close (47.4 against 44); from 8 up the Bridge is well below. Consolidating the baseline side (1 + m) is lower at every m. The crossover moves with and the density, which the CSV lets you explore.

Point-to-point grows with the product of the two sides, the Bridge with their sum. The count says nothing about how hard each interface is. The Bridge's interfaces are all concentrated in one component.

docs.title: 2. Change impact
docs.text:
uv run bridge-island experiment change-impact --seed 1 [--trials 1000]

Applies the v1 to v2 change set of the chosen example to both architectures and counts four things. The counting model is stated in the module docstring of bridge_island.analysis.change_impact. In short: every (element, subsystem) dependency has one conformance test, located in whatever owns the adapter for that dependency, and every subsystem has one acceptance test. The Bridge is re-verified after any baseline change.

Aviation, --seed 1:

Metric P2P Bridge Unique subsystems needing code change 3 1 Modules touched 3 2 Tests failing before the fix 9 7 Components needing re-verification 3 2

The "tests failing" row rests on an arbitrary assumption: that each dependency has exactly one conformance test (tests_per_edge = 1). Change that number and the row changes with it, but the gap between the architectures does not, because it equals the number of P2P subsystems with code changes minus the number of Bridge subsystems with code changes (3 - 1 = 2 here). The experiment writes the sensitivity to change_impact_sensitivity.csv:

Tests per dependency P2P tests failing Bridge tests failing 0 3 1 1 (the table above) 9 7 2 15 13 5 33 31

Read the other three rows with the same caution: they follow from the counting model, not from measurement.

For the Bridge, the code change is the Translator Module's mapping, except for the removed element: the one subsystem that used it must also handle the "unavailable" report. The re-verified components are the Bridge itself plus that subsystem.

The Monte Carlo mode draws random architectures (10 to 100 elements, 3 to 20 subsystems, density 0.1 to 0.6) and random change sets (1 to 6 changes of the six kinds), and reports distributions. With --seed 1 and 1000 trials, the mean [5th, 95th percentile] is:

Metric P2P Bridge Subsystems needing code change 6.0 [0, 15] 2.0 [0, 9] Modules touched 6.0 [0, 15] 2.9 [0, 10] Tests failing before the fix 14.9 [0, 42] 10.9 [0, 35] Components re-verified 7.8 [1, 17] 3.0 [1, 10]

Files: change_set.csv, change_impact.csv, change_impact_monte_carlo.csv, change_impact_distributions.csv, change_impact.png. The result depends on the counting model. Read it as a demonstration of where change lands, and change the model if you disagree with it.

docs.title: 3. Timing and continuity
docs.text:
uv run bridge-island experiment timing --seed 1

Stalls the Bridge for 1.5 s at t = 2.2 s, and runs the simulation twice: once with source time stamping (G3), once with the naive mode that stamps delivery time.

Time tag Max age of the held 1 Hz input Flagged late by the consumer Health events source (G3) about 0.7 s 1 bridge_stall, discontinuity delivery (naive) about 0 s 0 bridge_stall, discontinuity

While the Bridge is stalled, its buffer keeps only the latest message of each kind. When the Bridge resumes, a slow message that arrived mid-stall is released late. With source time the consumer sees how old it is and can reject it. Stamped with delivery time, it looks brand new, and the consumer cannot tell. In both runs the health monitor notices the gap in its own heartbeat (bridge_stall) and the jump in source times (discontinuity), and annunciates both to the affected subsystems, and consumers of fast data see the gap in the source times they received.

Files: timing_ages.csv (every datum with source time, delivery time and age), timing_summary.csv, timing.png.

docs.title: 4. Fault containment
docs.text:
uv run bridge-island experiment containment --seed 1

A unique subsystem sends a valid request, then four kinds of fault, on both architectures. The table is for the aviation example:

Scenario Bridge: baseline sees it? P2P: baseline sees it? valid message accepted accepted out-of-range value blocked by the Translator Module caught by the subsystem's own adapter code bad enum value blocked by the Translator Module caught by the subsystem's own adapter code malformed (missing field) blocked by the Translator Module caught by the subsystem's own adapter code unauthorized message type blocked and logged by the cyber monitor reaches the baseline, which rejects it baseline-format message, out of range blocked and logged by the cyber monitor reaches the baseline, which rejects it

On the Bridge the baseline's rejection count is zero in every scenario, and the Bridge's log records what it blocked and why. On P2P, a subsystem's own correct code stops the first three. When the subsystem's software is faulty, or sends something it should never send, the baseline has to deal with it directly.

File: containment.csv.

docs.title: Why this shape
docs.text: The baseline is fixed and certified elsewhere. The mission systems change at their own pace. The pattern puts the knowledge of how to bridge the two in one place, so that the part that must follow the baseline closely (the OIU and the mapping) is separate from the parts that follow each mission system. The six guidelines are what keep that separation honest. The architecture also follows the way the work is divided between the organizations, which is the observation behind Conway's paper: a structure that matches the authority boundaries is cheaper to keep than one that fights them.

docs.title: What the Bridge does not do
docs.text:
The Bridge concentrates complexity. It does not remove it. All the conversion, timing and protocol knowledge that used to be spread across subsystems now sits in one component. That component has to be correct, tested and kept current. The change-impact experiment shows the counts moving, not the work disappearing: the Bridge is re-verified after every baseline change, and the removed-element case still touches a unique subsystem. When a system has one or two subsystems and a stable baseline, point-to-point may well be cheaper. The experiments make no case for the Bridge at that scale.

The Bridge is a single point of failure and needs analysis. Every exchange passes through it. A stall, a crash or a wrong mapping affects every unique system at once. The health monitor detects a stall after the fact, as the timing experiment shows, but detection is not tolerance. This repository contains no redundancy, failover or fault-tree analysis of the Bridge. Anyone applying the pattern to a real system needs those, and a safety case for the Bridge itself.

The numbers are synthetic. All platforms, interfaces and rates are invented. The latency budgets, bus latencies and signal functions are arbitrary choices that make the behavior visible. The experiment counts follow a stated counting model, which is an assumption about where tests and adapters live, not a measurement of any real program. Do not quote the outputs as evidence about a real system.

It is not flight software or medical software, and it is not certified. It is a simulation for teaching, testing and discussion. It has not been analysed against any safety or certification standard and must not be used where failure could cause harm.

docs.title: Modelling limits
docs.text:
• The buses are simplified. The command/response, label-word and publish/subscribe models capture who may start a transfer, what the rate structure looks like, and a fixed latency. They have no arbitration, error detection, retries, jitter or bandwidth limits, and they are not implementations of any standard.
  • Python cannot enforce G1 absolutely. Code that misrepresents its own island can attach to the baseline. The design makes a bypass impossible through the public API, and the link registry makes any bypass visible. See Concepts.
  • Neither rate policy meets a need the baseline cannot supply. A subsystem that wants 50 Hz of data from a 20 Hz source cannot be fully served. cap delivers the real data at the rate the baseline has. extrapolate delivers the rate the interface expects, but part of it is predicted, and it adds latency. Either one keeps the existing interface working; neither meets the subsystem's full need. See Concepts. The extrapolator is deliberately simple (linear for floats, hold for other encodings, a short time limit) and is not a state estimator.
  • Time is simulated. The scheduler is deterministic and seeded. There is no wall-clock time, no clock drift between islands, and no clock synchronization problem. A real integration has all three.
  • The stall model is simple. A stalled Bridge keeps the latest message of each kind and drops uplinks. Other stall behaviors, such as queueing everything, would give different numbers.
  • Verification effort is counted, not costed. The counting model treats a test as a unit and an adapter as a module. It does not weigh the sizes of these things.

docs.title: Where the pattern fits less well
docs.text: It does not help when the baseline can be changed freely, when there is only one consumer, or when the unique systems can simply adopt the baseline's representation (guideline G2 still applies there: the Bridge passes the data through unchanged). It adds a component, a latency and a failure mode, and it is worth that only when the cost of coupling many independent systems to an immutable core is higher.

docs.title: Critical review: threats to validity
docs.text:
This section lists what the evidence in this repository does and does not show. All numbers here and elsewhere are synthetic, illustrative.

  • The platforms are invented, by design. Nothing here measures a real integration. The examples show that the behaviours are implemented and testable, not that the pattern pays off on any real system.
  • The change-impact model is a counting model. Its tests-per-dependency figure is an assumption, and the result depends on it (the sensitivity table shows how). The n it counts is baseline data elements, not baseline systems.
  • Latency is simulated. Delays come from a seeded random model, not from a measured bus. The average and peak ages are exact for the simulated deliveries, but the delay distribution is invented.
  • Neither rate policy meets a subsystem's full need. cap lowers the rate and extrapolate fills the gap with estimates (marked estimated). Both only support the existing interface.
  • Age is measured four ways because arrival age alone hides how long a value is held. The time-average and peak figures are the ones to read when a source is slow or the Bridge stalls.
  • Tests are checked by deliberate breakage. scripts/mutation_check.py changes the code on purpose and reports the changes no test notices. A sample run exposed gaps (an unconverted constant, exact counters, health thresholds); each was fixed or covered by a test. Some surviving mutants are equivalent changes that cannot be detected, so the score is not 100%.
  • One implementation, one author's model. The guidelines G1 to G6 are checked against this code, not against independent implementations.

docs.title: Policy and oversight context
docs.text:
Modular open systems approaches are required for many U.S. defense programs by statute, and recent oversight work reports on how that has gone. These sources describe the policy setting. They do not describe this repository, and this repository does not implement any program's approach.

  • 10 U.S.C. § 4401, "Requirement for modular open system approach in major defense acquisition programs; definitions". https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/10/4401
  • U.S. Government Accountability Office, Weapon Systems Acquisition: DOD Needs Better Planning to Attain Benefits of Modular Open Systems, GAO-25-106931, January 22, 2025. https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-25-106931

docs.title: Background on modularity and mediation
docs.text:
• D. L. Parnas, "On the criteria to be used in decomposing systems into modules," Communications of the ACM, vol. 15, no. 12, pp. 1053-1058, December 1972. doi:10.1145/361598.361623. Decomposing around design decisions that are likely to change, not around processing steps. The Bridge applies this to the baseline's interface: the part that must follow the baseline is isolated from everything else.
  • C. Y. Baldwin and K. B. Clark, Design Rules, Volume 1: The Power of Modularity. MIT Press, 2000. Design rules and hidden modules: independent teams can change what is hidden behind a stable interface.
  • G. Wiederhold, "Mediators in the architecture of future information systems," IEEE Computer, vol. 25, no. 3, pp. 38-49, March 1992. doi:10.1109/2.121508. A mediator is a module between data resources and their users that holds the knowledge needed to bridge their differences. The Bridge is a mediator in this sense. (Some reference lists spell the title "Mediation in the Architecture of Future Information Systems".)
  • M. E. Conway, "How do committees invent?," Datamation, vol. 14, no. 4, pp. 28-31, April 1968. Systems tend to mirror the communication structure of the organizations that build them.

docs.title: Related patterns, measures and standards
docs.text:
These were checked against their public pages. No claim is made that this project implements or conforms to any standard listed here.

  • The anti-corruption layer. The pattern places a layer between subsystems that do not share semantics, so that one can stay unchanged without compromising the design of the other. It was first described by Eric Evans in Domain-Driven Design: Tackling Complexity in the Heart of Software. "Anti-Corruption Layer Pattern", Azure Architecture Center, Microsoft Learn. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/anti-corruption-layer. The Bridge is the closest industry analogue, and the same page lists the costs this project documents: added latency, an extra component to operate, enforcing input validation at a boundary between different trust levels, observability to diagnose translation failures, and keeping business rules out of the layer. It also says the pattern may not suit systems without significant semantic differences, which matches the limits stated here.
  • Age of information. S. Kaul, R. Yates and M. Gruteser, "Real-time status: How often should one update?," in Proc. IEEE INFOCOM, 2012, pp. 2731-2735. Introduced the age of information as a measure of freshness. It is why this project reports the average and peak age over time, not only the age at arrival.
  • Valid time and transaction time. C. S. Jensen and C. E. Dyreson (eds.), "The Consensus Glossary of Temporal Database Concepts - February 1998 Version." The vocabulary for what G3 does: the source time is the valid time of a fact, and the delivery time is the time the system learned of it. https://infolab.usc.edu/csci599/Fall2001/paper/glossary.pdf (a copy of the glossary).
  • Design structure and propagation cost. A. MacCormack, J. Rusnak and C. Y. Baldwin, "Exploring the structure of complex software designs: An empirical study of open source and proprietary code," Management Science, vol. 52, no. 7, pp. 1015-1030, 2006. doi:10.1287/mnsc.1060.0552. Uses design structure matrices of element-to-element dependencies, as the dependency edges counted in the experiments are, and defines a propagation-cost measure of how far a change can spread. This project counts one-step dependencies; it does not compute propagation cost.
  • Medical device integration. ASTM F2761-09(2013), Medical Devices and Medical Systems - Essential safety requirements for equipment comprising the patient-centric integrated clinical environment (ICE) - Part 1: General requirements and conceptual model. A standard about integrating equipment from different manufacturers into one patient-centric system. The medical example is a structural illustration only and makes no clinical claim.
  • A published open avionics architecture. The FACE Approach, The Open Group. It defines a Reference Architecture, which includes a Transport Services Segment, and a Data Architecture. https://www.opengroup.org/face. It separates how data is moved from how it is represented, as this project separates the native-protocol ports from the Translator Module.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
A scenario is one YAML file that describes one reproducible run: which example, which baseline version, how long, what the Bridge's settings are, and what happens during the run. You can explore the behaviour of the Bridge without writing Python. This is also the recommended way to share a run: the file is the whole experiment.

uv run bridge-island run examples/scenarios/stall_and_resume.yaml

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
name: stall_and_resume
description: The Bridge stalls for 1.5 s. The health monitor annunciates it.
example: aviation            # required: aviation | medical
duration_s: 8                # required: simulated seconds
version: 1                   # baseline interface version (default: the first)
seed: 1                      # default 1
bridge:                      # optional Bridge settings
  time_tag: source           # source (G3) | delivery (the naive error)
  rate_policy: cap           # cap | extrapolate
  processing_delay_s: 0.001
  max_extrapolation_s: 0.2   # default: 1.5 source periods
events:                      # optional, each with a time `at` and exactly one action
  - {at: 2.2, stall: 1.5}                       # stall the Bridge for 1.5 s
  - at: 1.0                                     # a subsystem sends a message toward the baseline
    send: {from: PlanningDisplay, message: show_page, values: {page: MAP, priority: 1}}

Unknown keys, a time after the end of the run, a missing field, a sender that is not a subsystem and a baseline version the example does not have are all rejected with a message that says what to fix. A send may name any message, valid or not. That is how you inject a fault.

docs.title: Shipped scenarios
docs.text: File What it shows stall_and_resume.yaml The Bridge stalls for 1.5 s. The health monitor reports bridge_stall, and the 1 Hz message held through the stall arrives visibly old (flagged late). naive_time_stamping.yaml The same stall with delivery-time stamping, the error G3 forbids: nothing is flagged late, because the old data looks new. Compare the late column with the file above. baseline_v2_removal.yaml Baseline v2 removes an element. The subsystem that used it is told the input is unavailable. extrapolate_rate_policy.yaml A 50 Hz subsystem fed by a 20 Hz source, with estimates filling the gaps. fault_injection.yaml A faulty add-on module in the medical example sends one valid request and three bad ones (out of range, an unauthorized message type, a baseline-format message). The Bridge blocks the three, and the baseline sees none.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
uv run bridge-island run SCENARIO.yaml --json          # the summary and the manifest on stdout
uv run bridge-island run SCENARIO.yaml --trace t.csv   # every delivered datum
uv run bridge-island run SCENARIO.yaml --out results/  # summary.json, manifest.json, trace.csv

The trace has one row per datum a subsystem received: subsystem, input, source_time, basis_time (set for estimates), delivered_at, age_s and estimated. Its first line is # synthetic, illustrative.

The manifest records what is needed to reproduce the run: the package and Python versions, the resolved scenario (seed, baseline version, Bridge settings, events) and the SHA-256 of the mapping spec in use. It contains no wall-clock time, so running the same scenario twice gives the same manifest, summary and trace, byte for byte.

docs.title: Try it in your browser
docs.text:
You can run the app without installing anything: open the in-browser app.

It is the same app as bridge-island ui, with the same pages (run a simulation, scenario files, full report, guideline checks, experiments, help). Python runs inside your browser using Pyodide. Nothing you enter is uploaded, and nothing is saved unless you download it.

What to expect:

  • The first visit downloads about 10 MB (Python for the browser); the browser keeps it, so later visits start faster.
  • A long simulation takes longer than on your own computer, because Python in a browser is slower. The page stays responsive while it runs.
  • The experiment plots are not drawn in the browser (they need matplotlib); the tables and the CSV files are. For the plots, run the app on your own computer: see Using the app.
  • It needs a current browser with JavaScript and WebAssembly (any recent Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari).

All content is invented and all numbers are synthetic, illustrative.

docs.title: Tutorial: integrate a new unique subsystem in 15 minutes
docs.text:
You will add an invented subsystem, RangeEstimator, to the aviation example. It wants the airspeed in metres per second and the bus voltage, over publish/subscribe. You will touch three things: the subsystem's declared inputs, the mapping spec, and one command. You will not touch the baseline, the Bridge, or any other subsystem.

Work in a checkout of the repository, in examples/aviation_invented/. (Every step below is executed by the test suite, in tests/test_tutorial.py, so these snippets stay correct.)

docs.title: 1. Declare what the subsystem needs
docs.text:
In world.py, add its inputs to _needs(), in the subsystem's own units and protocol. Each n(...) is: native name, encoding, units, frame, protocol, highest useful rate in Hz, latency budget in seconds, and how old data may be when used, in seconds.

        "RangeEstimator": (
            n("airspeed_ms", "float64", "m/s", "air", PS, 1, 1.0, 5.0),
            n("bus_voltage_v", "float64", "V", "bus", PS, 1, 1.0, 5.0),
        ),

Then register its native protocol in _PROTOCOLS:

_PROTOCOLS = {..., "StatusLogger": CR, "RangeEstimator": PS}

docs.title: 2. Say how each input maps from the baseline
docs.text:
In both mapping_v1.yaml and mapping_v2.yaml, add two lines under downlinks::

  - {from: AirData.airspeed_kt, to: RangeEstimator.airspeed_ms, transforms: [{unit: [kt, m/s]}]}
  - {from: PowerStatus.bus_voltage_v, to: RangeEstimator.bus_voltage_v}

The first converts knots to metres per second. The second needs no conversion: the voltage representation matches, so the entry has no transforms and the value passes through unchanged (guideline G2).

docs.title: 3. Compile the mapping
docs.text:
uv run bridge-island codegen --spec examples/aviation_invented/mapping_v1.yaml
uv run bridge-island codegen --spec examples/aviation_invented/mapping_v2.yaml

The generator checks the spec against the baseline interface and your declared inputs, and writes generated/mapping_v*.py. It fails loudly if something does not fit. For example, if you did step 1 but forgot step 2:

codegen failed: RangeEstimator.airspeed_ms is a declared input but has no mapping entry

Other build-time failures: an element the baseline does not publish, a conversion where none is needed, a chain of conversions that does not reach the target units, or a transform that is not in the permitted set.

docs.title: 4. Run it
docs.text:
uv run bridge-island demo aviation
uv run bridge-island check-rules

The demo table now has a RangeEstimator row, with its own received count and data age. All six guideline checks still pass. Nothing else changed: the other subsystems show the same numbers as before.

docs.title: What you did not have to do
docs.text:
• You did not change the baseline interface. It is immutable to you.
  • You did not write protocol code. The UID opened a publish/subscribe connection for the new subsystem because _PROTOCOLS says so.
  • You did not write time-tag handling. Every value arrives with its source time, and the subsystem's data-age checks work immediately (RangeEstimator.check() reports missing or stale inputs).
  • You did not touch the other four subsystems or re-test them. When the baseline moves from v1 to v2, only the mapping lines change.

docs.title: If your subsystem sends data to the baseline
docs.text: Declare an Output (see PlanningDisplay.show_page in world.py) and add an uplinks: entry that maps each field to a field of a message the baseline accepts. The cyber monitor will allow exactly that message from that subsystem and block everything else, and the Translator Module will reject out-of-range or malformed values before they reach the baseline. See the containment experiment.
